column5: Course says UNIA 'mobilised millions' in the 1920s. Editor's introduction says Garvey's own membership estimates (two million) were imprecise and likely exaggerated by his own admission and by careful observers: say 'claimed millions' and tag ESTIMATE

UNIA founded in Jamaica 1914 (Garvey returned from England 1914, inspired by Washington's Up from Slavery); moved to New York 1916; Du Bois called Garvey the most dangerous enemy of the Negro race in America (editor's quote); course's Garvey/Du Bois disagreement stands

Garvey's 1922 meeting with Ku Klux Klan and 'racial purity' stance, Black Star Line collapse 1922, mail fraud conviction 1923, deportation 1927, never allowed into any African country, Liberia refused the UNIA settlement, 1934-37 admiration of Hitler/Mussolini: needed for a fair Module 3 lesson on Garvey's critics (Du Bois critique rests on real grounds)

Garvey died 10/06/1940 in London, reburied in Jamaica 1964; influence on Nkrumah and Kenyatta stated by editor (Nkrumah said the Philosophy and Opinions fired his enthusiasm); Red Black and Green flag introduced at 1920 convention

Garvey's own 1923 autobiographical claims: UNIA founded Jamaica five days after his arrival on 15/07/1914; arrived in US 23/03/1916; membership claims 2,000,000 by June 1919, 4,000,000 by Aug 1920, 6,000,000 and 900 branches in 1923 (self-reported, unverifiable; use as a lesson in reading a leader's own numbers); about 25,000 packed Madison Square Garden on 01/08/1920; Black Star Line incorporated 27/06/1919, suspended Dec 1921; he calls his trial a frame-up (partisan voice, needs the editor's counter-view)

Closing address to the jury, 15/06/1923: primary source for voice: he frames Atlantic slavery as the reason for the Black diaspora's displacement, says Garvey is an Irish slave-master's name (his own claim), and ties the Black Star Line to the Africa redemption plan; uses the 400,000,000 figure for Black people worldwide (rhetorical)

Declaration of the Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World, adopted at the 1920 convention (01 to 31/08/1920; sworn 15/08/1920): twelve complaints and 54 articles, claiming to speak for 'four hundred million Negroes'. Complaint III protests the European partition of Africa; Article 13 demands 'Africa for the Africans at home and abroad'; Articles 7 and 8 reject land alienation and taxation without representation; Article 39 sets Red Black and Green as the race colours; Article 45 declares the League of Nations void for Negroes. Primary source for Module 3 lesson 1 (voice of Garvey) and a link to Module 1 (hut tax, land)

Article 47 and Article 16: Garvey's Declaration justifies war to defend rights and claims no Negro should fight for an alien race without his leader's consent: shows UNIA politics were state-like and assertive, a good contrast with Congress demands for fair treatment (Du Bois 1919-1927)

Speech at Liberty Hall 11/02/1921: Garvey ties Black Star Line and a 'Universal Liberian Construction Loan' to emigration to Liberia as the answer to post-war unemployment (a ship costing about 500,000 dollars is discussed). Shows the scheme was framed as an economic-emigration plan, and that he already called Du Bois' circle false leaders. Good for a worked example on Garvey's programme versus Du Bois' demands for rights

Speech 23/07/1921 'Leadership': Garvey attacks Du Bois and Moton as 'old leadership' that accepts philanthropy and industrial schools; claims 2,000,000 Black soldiers fought in the war and 50,000 delegates would attend the 1921 convention (his figures; Black military service numbers and attendance are not verified here). Primary voice for the Garvey versus Du Bois contrast in Module 3 lesson 1; gives Garvey's side of the quarrel so the lesson is balanced

Closing speech of the 1921 convention, 31/08/1921: Garvey protests the League of Nations division of former German territory in West Africa between France and Britain (he gives 608,000 square miles, his figure, unverified here) without consulting Black people: a primary voice linking Pan-Africanism to Module 1/2 (mandates, partition). Also cites Liberia being 'circumvented'. Comparative voice beside Du Bois' 1919 Congress asking for fair treatment

Speech 14/08/1921: 'Africa for the Africans' cry framed as the universal Negro answer to oppression, comparing the aim to US, French and Russian revolutions; pledge to plant the Red Black and Green on Africa: use as a short primary-source reading with the course's note that Garvey never entered an African country

01/01/1922 Emancipation Day speech and 13/01/1922 arrest statement: Garvey claims 4.5 million and over 4 million UNIA members (self-reported, rising claim each year; do not repeat as fact); frames Africa's liberation as the debt owed to enslaved ancestors

Speech 13/02/1922: Garvey endorses a Mississippi state senator's resolution (reported 31/01/1922) urging the US to secure African territory as a home for Black Americans; he welcomes support from segregationists, saying the UNIA and the senator share a goal. This is the concrete ground for critics such as Du Bois (that Garvey's emigration plan colluded with white racists): use as an evidence-based example in the Garvey critics section, without claiming more than the text shows

Course lesson 1 gives 'Africa for the Africans' as Garvey's slogan without saying what he meant. In his open letter of 18/04/1922 the phrase means that Black people from the whole world should build a nation in Africa, with diaspora settlers expected to work in partnership with native Africans and not as overlords; he welcomes help from US senators and a former German governor's suggestion that America take over mandates. So the slogan was a diaspora colonisation-and-nation plan, not a statement of self-rule by existing African peoples. Add one sentence and a short source reading to Module 3 lesson 1

Speech 09/07/1922 on his meeting with the Ku Klux Klan's acting Imperial Wizard in Atlanta on 25/06/1922: Garvey says the Klan speaks for white America, equates the UNIA aim (Africa a Black man's country) with the Klan's aim (America a white man's country), and urges Black leaders to understand rather than fight the Klan. This is a primary source for why Du Bois and the NAACP condemned him; the course should state the facts of the meeting and the reaction, and not endorse either reading

Opening address, third UNIA convention, 01/08/1922: Garvey cites Pan-African ferment from press reports (Reuters in January 1922 on Pan-African spirit in South Africa, Uganda, Nyasaland, Belgian Congo, Abyssinia, Kenya), the Rif war against Spain (his casualty numbers are reported claims, treat as unverified), a Kenya rising in 1922 (his account, secondhand; the course should not repeat it as fact) and Rene Maran's 1921 Goncourt for Batouala attacking colonial rule. Shows how colonial news reached the diaspora; useful as a source-criticism example in Module 3

Garvey reports (01/08/1922) that the League of Nations Council met in London in July 1922 and apportioned the former German colonies: parts of Cameroon to Britain and France, Togoland to France, East Africa to Britain. A contemporary Black diaspora reaction to mandates; a short primary-source line for Module 1 (what rule looked like afterwards) and Module 3

Speech 13/08/1922: Garvey attacks critics Pickens, Du Bois, Weldon Johnson, Owen and Randolph by name, rejects socialism as another form of white control, and argues that talk about Africa as a savage place was colonial propaganda meant to justify partition. Good voice for the point that the diaspora disagreed among itself (Garvey versus NAACP/Socialist wing), so 'Pan-Africanism' was never one programme (already in the course)

Speech 25/11/1922 'Principles of the UNIA': Garvey says the UNIA is 'nation building', not church or social work, and that unlike other organisations it seeks independence rather than a secondary place inside white-ruled states. His 400,000,000 splits into 15 million in the US, 180 million in Asia, the West Indies and the Americas and 200 million in Africa: self-estimated and loose; use as an example of a leader's rhetorical numbers in Module 3 lesson 1 (units: who is counted as 'Negro')

13/02/1923 reply to Du Bois' article 'Back to Africa' (Century Magazine, February 1923): Garvey answers Du Bois' physical description and charge that the UNIA was a poor enterprise with personal abuse and a colour-caste argument (he claims Du Bois favours light-skinned people and philanthropy). Shows the quarrel was personal and about class and colour in the diaspora as well as about method; supports the course's 'Du Bois and others criticised Garvey' but the lesson should name the real article (Du Bois, 'Back to Africa', Century, Feb 1923) and say Garvey's rebuttal is polemic, not neutral evidence. Insults not to be quoted

Garvey (23/04/1923) quotes an editorial of 29/03/1923 from Abantu-Batho, the Johannesburg paper of the South African Native National Congress (ANC), on the Cape Coloured people, whom white politicians were courting as a 'buffer' and who were urged to classify themselves as Africans: a rare primary trace of 1920s South African racial politics, from before apartheid, that fits Module 5 lesson 1 (earlier segregation). Secondhand quotation in Garvey's text, so cite as 'quoted by Garvey'

Speeches of 20 and 22/05/1923 (as the mail-fraud trial opened): Garvey treats the Black Star Line failure as a plot by enemies and the trial as a trial of the UNIA's principles. Garvey's version of events, set against the editor's note that the line was badly run; keep the two readings side by side

31/08/1923 'Caste System among Negroes' (written in the Tombs): Garvey accuses Du Bois and the NAACP of a colour-caste plot, i.e. the dispute was framed by Garvey as one of colour and class in the diaspora. Partisan source; use only to show how the quarrel was argued, not to judge the NAACP

11/09/1923 first speech after release on bail: Garvey himself describes the conviction as for selling Black Star Line stock after it was insolvent, with a sentence of five years and a fine of 1,000 dollars, and says co-defendants went free; he says the line was cheated by others (a 25,000 dollar and 11,000 dollar payment for the Phyllis Wheatley that never became a ship). Gives the conviction details from the defendant's side; the course may say 'convicted of mail fraud in 1923 (five years), which he and supporters called a frame-up and historians describe as the product of poor management plus federal hostility (editor)'

Speech 04/06/1924 sending an advance party to Liberia: land grants (25 acres per family, 15 single, 10 a woman, 5 per child) and a colonist sailing planned for September 1924. Editor's introduction says Liberia, under pressure from European governments, refused the UNIA a settlement. So the Liberia plan was concrete but never carried out; Module 3 can state this with the primary source for the plan and the editor for the outcome. Garvey also describes the Liberian ruling class as Americo-Liberians descended from American settlers (a detail the course never mentions)

Editor's footnote 40 (Dover edition): Garvey 'misstated or misunderstood' Liberia's position; Liberia neither invited nor allowed settlement by UNIA members. Confirms the outcome for the Liberia plan; Garvey's own 1924 speech claimed an invitation
Publisher's catalogue (Dover Thrift list): no content for the course

Editor's note: the 1921 resolution protested the distribution of Africa's land among white nations by the Supreme Council and League of Nations and was carried unanimously (convention of 31/08/1921). Supports Module 3 and Module 1 mandate point
